title: Transformer-Based Characterization of Criticality in Directed Percolation
abstract: Directed percolation (DP) provides a canonical framework for studying nonequilibrium phase transitions into absorbing states, yet extracting critical behavior directly from high-dimensional spatiotemporal configurations remains challenging. Here, we investigate (1 + 1)- and (2 + 1)-dimensional bond DP using a supervised Transformer encoder. Supervised learning results demonstrate that the Transformer can distinguish between the active and absorbing phases of directed percolation with high accuracy. The critical point and critical exponents estimated from the model's classification probabilities align closely with reference values from existing literature, indicating that the model not only achieves phase classification but also yields outputs containing information related to critical scaling behavior. To probe the model's internal representation, we employ attention rollout and define an attention center that quantifies the temporal centroid of the cumulative attention distribution. The attention patterns and the attention center reorganize systematically near the critical region and exhibit pronounced finite-size dependence. Finally, we examined the model's transferability between configurations generated from fully occupied initial states and those from single-seed initial states. The results indicate the presence of transferable information between the two types of data, though the transfer performance exhibits directional asymmetry. Furthermore, when using an equal amount of target-domain data, fine-tuning yielded only a marginal improvement in accuracy compared to training from scratch.

title: Immobilisation and remobilisation of surfactant-covered drop interfaces in electric fields: Simulations
abstract: Fluid--fluid interfaces are seldom clean due to the presence of surfactants, which can strongly modify their dynamics. Interfacial flow redistributes surfactant, creating concentration gradients whose Marangoni stresses can immobilise the interface. By contrast, surface diffusion or exchange with the bulk can reduce these gradients and restore interfacial motion. We study this competition using a two-dimensional model of a surfactant-covered leaky-dielectric drop in a uniform electric field. Electric stresses drive the classical Taylor circulation, in which the drop remains non-rotating. At stronger fields, convection of interfacial charge can destabilise this state and produce the Quincke regime, characterised by spontaneous mean rotation. Using a fully nonlinear model on a fixed circular interface, we show that weak surfactant diffusion allows Marangoni stresses to suppress the Taylor circulation almost completely. Quincke rotation remobilises this nearly arrested interface and restores a substantial straining circulation, whose orientation varies with the applied field. Surfactant also shifts the critical field for rotation and can change the onset from subcritical to supercritical. Surface diffusion and exchange with a well-mixed bulk reservoir can produce similar flow responses and rotation thresholds despite different surfactant distributions. The spatial variation of surfactant concentration therefore provides additional information for distinguishing the two transport mechanisms.

title: Electrohydrodynamic interactions of two Quincke rotors: asymptotic theory and boundary element simulations
abstract: Weakly conducting spheres suspended in a leaky dielectric fluid can undergo spontaneous Quincke rotation when the applied electric field exceeds a critical value. We investigate how electric and hydrodynamic interactions modify this instability and the subsequent rotation of two spheres at fixed separation and orientation. Starting from electric dipole and hydrodynamic rotlet interactions, we develop a systematic far-field asymptotic theory. Away from onset, slow drift of the rotation axes makes a regular expansion fail at long times. A multiple-scale expansion gives slow phase equations that select the axes according to pair orientation and field strength. Near onset, weak interactions produce corrections comparable to the isolated rotation magnitude. A detuned multiple-scale expansion gives coupled equations for the transverse dipole amplitudes. Their linearization identifies four collective rotation modes, whose critical fields and steady branches with one active mode are determined together with their stability. At leading order near onset, electric interaction shifts all four modal thresholds equally, whereas hydrodynamic interaction makes counter-rotation appear first for pair angles below $\cos^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)\simeq54.7^\circ$ and co-rotation above it. Away from onset, the angle separating stable counter-rotation from stable co-rotation increases with field strength. Boundary element method (BEM) simulations place onset within a field interval for each configuration and resolve the growth and relaxation of rotation. Steady-speed comparisons show how pair orientation changes the balance between electric and hydrodynamic effects. We compare the unexpanded dipole-rotlet model of Das and Saintillan [Phys. Rev. E 87, 043014 (2013)] with our asymptotic theory and BEM simulations.

title: Enforcing Symmetries on Pre-trained ML Models for Physics
abstract: Post-hoc group averaging (or test-time augmentation) is a simple way to impose symmetry on a trained predictor without changing its architecture or retraining it. For finite and compact groups, averaging over a normalized Haar measure on the group gives the Reynolds operator: a canonical projection onto invariant or equivariant predictors with known non-increasing risk guarantees under certain assumptions. This paper provides numerical experiments on physics emulation models that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach in this setting. We then extend this framework to non-compact group symmetries. For non-compact groups, the Haar measure cannot be normalized, so group averaging cannot be defined in the same way. We replace it with three alternatives: the Weyl unitary trick (which requires complexifying the space and extending the predictor), a data-dependent orthogonal projection (which involves a non-trivial optimization on the space of invariant or equivariant functions), and a frame averaging approach (which involves mapping each point to a set of orbit representatives). We illustrate the constructions theoretically and empirically on the unit-rescaling group and the Lorentz group. Our results show that in the non-compact case, the Weyl trick and frame averaging do not provide a consistent improvement over the baseline, except where the test data is out-of-distribution (an orders-of-magnitude improvement in this case) and, for the Weyl trick, in low-data regimes. The orthogonal projection can provide improvements in-distribution and out-of-distribution. We also observe that models trained directly on invariant features matched or beat the projection of an unconstrained one. We conclude that post-hoc symmetrization extends to non-compact groups, but it does not consistently outperform training a symmetric model.

title: Low-Rank Iteration for Efficient Calculations of Topological Surface States
abstract: Surface states are hallmarks of topological phases, and their efficient computation is crucial for topology characterization. Conventional supercell methods (SCM) approximate semi-infinite systems as finite periodic ones, but suffer from high computational cost, artificial inter-surface coupling, and slow convergence near band edges. Recently, boundary problems for semi-infinite systems have been recast as block-tridiagonal equations and solved by the cyclic reduction method (CRM) and the transfer matrix method (TMM). However, these approaches remain resource-intensive, as fine-mesh discretization produces very large matrices. Recognizing the intrinsic sparsity and low rank of these matrices, we develop a low-rank iterative method (LIM) with stochastic trace estimation that substantially reduces complexity and memory without sacrificing accuracy, while remaining straightforwardly parallelizable. Benchmarks on 2D and 3D topological systems show orders-of-magnitude acceleration over CRM and TMM. LIM extends readily to heterostructures, defective interfaces, and non-Hermitian systems, providing an efficient platform for topological and plasmonic surface phenomena.

title: Complex Hyperspin Machine and Symmetry Quenching: Benchmark and scaling up to millions of degrees of freedom
abstract: Driven-dissipative oscillator networks have been proposed to simulate spin models on physical hardware, mostly focusing on systems of binary (Ising) spins, or systems of spin vectors in low dimensions. The equalized hyperspin machine was recently introduced to provide a single platform to simulate general models of $N$ coupled spin vectors with tunable dimension $D$, realizing dynamical annealing protocols to vary the spin dimensionality in time. These schemes are limited to real spins coupled via real coupling matrices. We propose a generalization of the hyperspin machine that works with complex fields and deals with complex Hermitian coupling matrices, implementing an amplitude equalization scheme. This system, which we name complex hyperspin machine, can work on optimization problems with complex valued hyperspins that can be cast on complex $D$-vector Hamiltonians. We benchmark the machine against a differential evolution (DE) algorithm on complex $D=2$ hyperspins up to $N=80$, showing that the fraction of instances where a lower-energy solution is found grows with system size and coupling density, reaching $92.5\%$ at the largest considered sizes. When the DE finds a lower-energy solution, the machine still reaches a median relative energy deviation that lies between $10^{-15}$ and $10^{-12}$ while running at substantially lower computational cost. Using the complex nature of the field, we introduce a new dimensional reduction protocol that we name symmetry quenching, which collapses complex variables that map to XY spins onto real Ising spins by switching on the parametric pump. We show on Max-Cut instances with known ground states that symmetry quenching outperforms a fixed-pump Ising machine, reaching exact ground states in the presence of equalization. We scale the system to $N=10^6$ hyperspins, or $8\times10^6$ dynamical variables, on a Hermitian sparse two-dimensional lattice.

title: Physics Informed Priors for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials with Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Standard uncertainty quantification methods for machine learning interatomic potentials often fail to quantify the effects of model misspecification despite its prominence as a source of error. To combat this, misspecification-aware uncertainty schemes have been gaining attention, pointwise optimal parameter set regression (POPS-Regression) among them. However, no guarantees on the physicality of the posterior distribution are given and uncertainty estimates can be conservative compared to the true error. To combat this, we present a model misspecification aware scheme that builds on POPS-Regression by allowing users to specify physical priors that are enforced across the obtained ensemble of models. This allows the user to incorporate misspecification-aware uncertainties without compromising on physical properties. The scheme is applicable to any physical quantity that can be represented by a convex set of parameters and so is robust for a wide variety of static properties which can help inform dynamical simulations. Here, we demonstrate the scheme for phononic vibrations and elastic properties. The scheme is also applied to both linear and message-passing neural network potentials by exploiting the linearity available in both architectures; for neural network potentials we approximate the readout layer as a linear model based on fixed non-linear features. The versatility of the method provides an alternative to hand-crafted or active learning approaches to data-set construction to correct physical failures by adding data thus reducing the computational overhead for designing potentials for specific applications.

title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media
abstract: Coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) models describe interactions among displacement, fluid pressure, and temperature in geothermal systems. Fine-mesh simulations over many time steps are costly, particularly with heterogeneous permeability and thermal conductivity or fracture networks that alter fluid and heat transport. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduces the number of unknowns but can require many modes because its reconstruction is linear. We apply SparseModesNet to reconstruct coupled THM solutions using a small set of selected modes and a neural-network nonlinear decoder. Starting from a larger collection of candidate modes, SparseModesNet selects modes to reduce reconstruction error rather than simply retaining those with the highest energy. We compare SparseModesNet with POD on three problems: a two-dimensional heterogeneous medium, a two-dimensional connected fracture network, and a three-dimensional geometry based on Utah FORGE fractures. We evaluate reconstructed displacement, pressure, and temperature fields, as well as pressure- and temperature-based quantities of interest. We also test temporal interpolation by training on a subset of snapshots and reconstructing omitted snapshots within the same time interval. For the same reduced dimension, SparseModesNet achieves smaller reconstruction errors than POD and accurately recovers the solution fields and selected geothermal quantities of interest.

title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
abstract: Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.
